intro.eyebrow: MARVI:  Managing Aquifer Recharge & Sustaining Groundwater Use through Village level intervention
intro.title: What is MARVI?
intro.lede: MARVI puts groundwater science in the hands of the people who depend on it—farmers, schools, researchers and communities working together for water that lasts!

heroImage.alt: Community members and researchers discussing a groundwater map

left.lead: The aim is to improve irrigation-water security and rural livelihoods by making the invisible visible.

paragraphs: Groundwater is often managed one well at a time, even though every bore draws from a connected aquifer. MARVI creates a shared picture through participatory monitoring, aquifer-recharge assessment and village dialogue.
The project works across hydrology, hydrogeology, agronomy, economics and social science. The result is not a report left on a shelf, but knowledge a community can use.

blocks.title: Why groundwater?
blocks.lede: Rain moves through soil and rock into an aquifer. Wells reveal only a small window into a connected underground system.

items.title: The aquifer is shared
items.text: Water pumped from one well can affect neighbours drawing from the same underground store.

items.title: Rainfall is not recharge
items.text: Only part of rain reaches groundwater; soils, geology, land use and structures shape the journey.

items.title: Trends need time
items.text: A single reading is a snapshot. Repeated measurements reveal depletion, recovery and seasonal rhythm.

blocks.quote: How can a village understand an invisible shared resource—and decide its future together?

blocks.title: Where MARVI works
blocks.lede: MARVI acknowledges the women and men of the Dharta and Meghraj watersheds whose observations, experience and leadership shaped the project.

photo.alt: A Bhujal Jankaar measuring a village well

right.lead: A Bhujal Jankaar makes groundwater science legible—well by well, season by season, village by village.
paragraphs: These trained volunteers measure wells, rainfall, water quality and check dams. They interpret local patterns, explain them in the community’s own language and help farmers see that groundwater is both limited and shared.
